## Why this unit matters

- The conceptual anchor of the course: derive the SIR model of Kermack &
  McKendrick (1927) from first principles.
- Read off the two quantities that govern every epidemic: the reproduction
  number $R_0$ and the epidemic threshold.
- Solve it with the modern **SciML** stack and verify conservation, the
  threshold, and the analytic **final-size** relation.

## The SIR model and mass action {.smaller}

Closed, well-mixed population; constant recovery; permanent immunity.

A susceptible person's hazard of infection is transmission probability ×
contacts × prevalence:

$$
\lambda=\underbrace{\beta}_{\text{transmission probability}}\times
\underbrace{c}_{\text{contacts per day}}\times
\underbrace{\frac{I}{N}}_{\text{prevalence}}
$$

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}S}{\mathrm{d}t}=-\lambda S,\quad
\frac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t}=\lambda S-\gamma I,\quad
\frac{\mathrm{d}R}{\mathrm{d}t}=\gamma I.
$$ {#eq-s-ch01-sir}

::: {.notes}
Derive the mass-action term from contacts × prevalence × transmission
probability: each of the S susceptibles makes c dt contacts, a fraction I/N of
them are with infectious people, and each transmits with probability β.

Then sum the three right-hand sides at the board. The λS term appears once with
each sign, and so does γI, so everything cancels and d(S+I+R)/dt = 0 at every t.
Nothing in the code will enforce S+I+R = N. It holds because each equation was
written as a flow out of one compartment and into another. That is what the
conservation check later in the deck is testing.
:::

## $R_0$ and the epidemic threshold {.smaller}

$R_0$ is the expected number of secondary infections one infectious person
produces in a fully susceptible population. Factoring $\gamma I$ out of
@eq-s-ch01-sir gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}
R_0 &= \frac{\beta c}{\gamma},\\
\frac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t} &= \gamma I\Bigl(R_0\frac{S}{N}-1\Bigr) = \gamma I R_0\Bigl(\frac{S}{N}-\frac{1}{R_0}\Bigr).
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-s-ch01-r0}

During an active outbreak ($I > 0$), the susceptible fraction (s = $S/N$) governs the sign of the derivative, defining three phases:

- If $S/N>1/R_0 \Rightarrow \mathrm{d}I/\mathrm{d}t>0$ , active infections are growing
- If $S/N=1/R_0 \Rightarrow \mathrm{d}I/\mathrm{d}t=0$, marking the turning point where the epidemic reaches its peak
- If $S/N<1/R_0 \Rightarrow \mathrm{d}I/\mathrm{d}t<0$ , active infections are declining

::: {.notes}
S never increases, so R₀·S/N − 1 changes sign at most once: I rises and then
falls, with a single maximum rather than several.

Two things to say out loud. Growth is exponential only early on, while S is
close to N; once S is being depleted the growth is slower than that. And the
peak sits at S/N = 1/R₀ only when the epidemic grows first, that is, when
R₀·S(0)/N > 1, which holds here (1.98). If it does not, I falls from the start
and its largest value is I(0), at t = 0.
:::

## What is the final size of an epidemic in terms of surviving susceptibles? {.smaller}

We define population fractions $s = S/N$ and $r = R/N$. As $N$ is constant, their rates of change scale identically: $\frac{\mathrm{d}S}{\mathrm{d}R} = \frac{\mathrm{d}s}{\mathrm{d}r}$.

Dividing the rates of change in @eq-s-ch01-sir gives us:
$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}s}{\mathrm{d}r} = \frac{-\lambda S}{\gamma I} = \frac{-\beta c (I/N) S}{\gamma I} = -R_0 s.
$$

Separating variables and integrating from $t=0$ to a state:
$$
\int_{s_0}^{s} \frac{1}{y}\,\mathrm{d}y = -R_0 \int_{0}^{r} \mathrm{d}x \implies \ln\left(\frac{s}{s_0}\right) = -R_0 r.
$$

Exponentiating both sides gives $s(t) = s_0 e^{-R_0 r(t)}$. At the end nobody is
infectious, $i_\infty = 0$, and $s + i + r = 1$, so $r_\infty = 1 - s_\infty$:

$$
s_\infty = s_0 e^{-R_0 (1 - s_\infty)}.
$$ {#eq-s-ch01-finalsize}

::: {.notes}
Dividing is the chain rule: dS/dR = (dS/dt)/(dR/dt), valid while I > 0. The step
that makes it work is I cancelling between the two rates, which leaves an
equation in S and R with no time in it. That is why γ disappears here and why
the final size does not depend on how fast the epidemic runs.

In fractions it is ds/dr = −R₀·s, separable, so ds/s = −R₀ dr and integrating
from the start to the end gives s∞ = s₀ exp(−R₀·r∞). The last step only replaces
r∞.

Read the exponent as a quantity with meaning: R₀·r is the total force of
infection a susceptible has been exposed to by the time a fraction r has
recovered, and e^(−R₀r) is their chance of having escaped it. The last step just
says that at the end the recovered fraction is everyone who is not still
susceptible.

If some people are immune at the start, r₀ = R(0)/N is not zero and the exponent
becomes −R₀(1 − s∞ − r₀), because only those removed after t = 0 add to the
force of infection. The chapter does that case.
:::

## What does the final size tell us? {.smaller}
 
- *The Peak:* The outbreak stops growing when the susceptible fraction $S/N$ drops to $1/R_0$. 
- *The End:* Transmission only stops later when active cases run out, leaving a final susceptible fraction $s_\infty > 0$.

_Example:_ For $R_0 = 2$, the epidemic will peak at $1/R_0 = 1/2$ or 50% susceptible. However, the final size will be $s_\infty \approx 0.20$ or 20% susceptible. To get to this number you can numerically solve to find the root of the equation: 

$$
s_\infty = s_0 e^{-R_0 (1 - s_\infty)}
$$

Assuming $s_0 \approx 1$ (mostly susceptible at the start), we can calculate:

| Guess for $s_\infty$ | Calculate $(1)*\exp(-2(1-s_\infty))$ | Match? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0.50 | $\exp(-2(1-0.5)) \approx 0.368$ | No ($0.50 \neq 0.368$) |
| 0.30 | $\exp(-2(1-0.3)) \approx 0.247$ | No ($0.30 \neq 0.247$) |
| 0.20 | $\exp(-2(1-0.2)) \approx 0.202$ | Very close ($0.20 \approx 0.202$) |



::: {.notes}
Be careful with "ends" here. Two different things happen at two different times:
growth stops when S/N crosses 1/R₀, and transmission stops when I reaches zero,
long afterwards.

The gap between 0.50 and 0.20 is the part worth dwelling on. Prevalence is at
its highest at the instant S/N crosses the threshold, which is the whole
problem: the largest infectious pool of the epidemic then has to work its way
through, infecting as it recovers, so S is pushed well past the threshold before
I reaches zero. The epidemic overshoots the point where it stopped growing.

If someone asks, S/N = 1/R₀ is the herd immunity threshold, equivalently
1 − 1/R₀ = 50% immune here. The 20% never infected are protected by the immunity
of the people around them, not by anything about themselves. The overshoot is
why an unmitigated epidemic passes that threshold rather than settling at it.

No rearranging gives s∞ in closed form, since it appears on its own and inside
the exponential. It can be written with the Lambert W function, but here and
throughout the course we find the root numerically. That is NonlinearSolve on
the next slide, the same solve function as the ODE with a different problem type
selecting the method.

For the γ point, offer the test: double βc and γ together. R₀ is unchanged, both
right-hand sides scale by the same factor, so the trajectory traces the identical
path through (S, I, R) with the same peak of 158 infectious people and the same
s∞, but arrives in half the time. The worksheet solution does this.

The 80% counts the 1% seeded at t = 0 as well as those infected afterwards. The
chapter separates the three quantities that are easy to confuse here.
:::

## SciML ecosystem in Julia

High-performance, open-source software stack for scientific machine learning, combining differential equation solving, symbolic modeling, and machine learning into a single unified environment

- `OrdinaryDiffEq.jl`: Numerical solvers for ordinary differential equations (ODEs)
- `NonlinearSolve.jl`: Fast non-allocating implementations on static arrays of common methods (Newton-Rhapson)

## Solving Continuous Dynamics: OrdinaryDiffEq.jl {.smaller}

To trace an epidemic curve over time, we model the system as continuous flows using ordinary differential equations (ODEs)

Our model kernel, `sir_ode!`, is a derivative calculator:

```julia
function sir_ode!(du, u, p, t)
    S, I, R = u                       
    λ = p.β * p.c * I / p.N
    du[1] = -λ * S; du[2] = λ * S - p.γ * I; du[3] = p.γ * I; return nothing
end
```

To find the state of the population across a timespan, we must integrate these equations over time:

```julia
using OrdinaryDiffEq
sol = solve(ODEProblem(sir_ode!, u0, tspan, p), Tsit5(); saveat = 0.5)
```

The `solve` function takes the `ODEProblem` and and the solver (in this case `Tsit5()`) and returns an `ODESolution` object, which contains the integrated state of the population across the timespan.

## Solving nonlinear static finite element analysis: NonlinearSolve.jl {.smaller}

Sometimes, we do not need the full time-series trajectory of the epidemic. We only want to calculate the final state at the end of the outbreak (as $t \to \infty$)

$$
s_\infty = s_0 e^{-R_0 (1 - s_\infty)}
$$

```julia
using NonlinearSolve
sol = solve(NonlinearProblem((s, R0) -> s - s₀ * exp(-R0 * (1 - s)), 
        initial_guess, 
        R₀), NewtonRaphson()).u
```

Where `(s, R0) -> s - s₀ * exp(-R0 * (1 - s))` is the function solving for `s`. The `NewtonRaphson()` is the solver, `NonlinearProblem` is the problem type, and `solve` returns the final state `s_inf`.

## Comparing both solutions

```{julia}
#| label: s-ch01-solve
#| echo: true
using OrdinaryDiffEq, NonlinearSolve
function sir_ode!(du, u, p, t)
    S, I, R = u                       
    λ = p.β * p.c * I / p.N
    du[1] = -λ * S; du[2] = λ * S - p.γ * I; du[3] = p.γ * I; return nothing
end

u0 = [990.0, 10.0, 0.0]; tspan = (0.0, 80.0)
p  = (β = 0.05, c = 10.0, γ = 0.25, N = 1000.0)
sol = solve(ODEProblem(sir_ode!, u0, tspan, p), Tsit5(); saveat = 0.5)
R₀ = p.β * p.c / p.γ; s₀ = u0[1] / p.N
s_inf = solve(NonlinearProblem((s, R0) -> s - s₀ * exp(-R0 * (1 - s)), 0.2, R₀),
              NewtonRaphson()).u

println("From the ODEProblem, du[1][end]/N: $(round(sol.u[end][1] / p.N; digits = 3))")
println("From the NonlinearProblem, s_inf: $(round(s_inf; digits = 3))")
```

## Plotting the solutions from the ODEProblem

```{julia}
#| label: fig-s-ch01-sir
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "Baseline SIR ($R_0=2$). The dashed line marks $S/N=1/R_0$; the infectious curve peaks exactly where $S$ crosses it."
using CairoMakie
t = sol.t; S = sol[1, :]; I = sol[2, :]; R = sol[3, :]
fig = Figure(size = (760, 400))
ax = Axis(fig[1,1]; xlabel = "day", ylabel = "individuals", title = "SIR baseline, R₀ = 2")
lines!(ax, t, S; color = :steelblue, linewidth = 3, label = "S")
lines!(ax, t, I; color = :firebrick, linewidth = 3, label = "I")
lines!(ax, t, R; color = :seagreen,  linewidth = 3, label = "R")
hlines!(ax, [p.N / R₀]; color = :black, linestyle = :dash, label = "S = N/R₀")
axislegend(ax; position = :rc); fig
```

## Validation {.smaller}

- Does the epidemic cross the threshold to assume we are in the "growth" phase, $R_0 S(0)/N>1$? Yes,  $R_0 s_0 = 2 \times 990/1000 = 1.98$
- Is the population conserved?
- Is the peak at $S/N = 1/R_0$?
- Does the long-run $S/N$ match the analytic $s_\infty$? 

```{julia}
#| label: s-ch01-check
#| echo: true
cons = all(u -> isapprox(sum(u), p.N; atol = 1e-6), sol.u)
peak = isapprox(S[argmax(I)] / p.N, 1 / R₀; atol = 0.01)
sol_long = solve(ODEProblem(sir_ode!, u0, (0.0, 400.0), p), Tsit5();
                 reltol = 1e-10, abstol = 1e-10, save_everystep = false)
fsize = isapprox(sol_long.u[end][1] / p.N, s_inf; atol = 1e-3)
(cons, peak, fsize)
```

All `true`: conservation, peak at $S/N = 1/R_0$, and final size are confirmed.

::: {.notes}
Point back at the kernel: nothing in it says S + I + R = N, and the solver was
never told. Conservation holds because the equations were written as flows
between compartments, so the check is testing the model and the integration
tolerance rather than a constraint anyone imposed. The 1e-6 tolerance is there
because Tsit5 takes finite steps.

The threshold check is only meaningful because R₀·S(0)/N = 1.98 > 1, so the peak
is interior. Raising γ to 0.5 makes R₀ = 1, I falls from day zero, and argmax
returns the first index rather than a turning point. That is the second exercise
in the chapter.
:::

## Limitations 

- In an ODE model, state variables are continuous real numbers. If active infections ($I$) drop to a fraction of a person, $I < 1$, the epidemic remains mathematically alive. 
- A deterministic ODE does not account for super-spreading events or small-outbreak noise.
- We assume homogeneous mixing. An infectious individual on Day 10 is just as likely to infect a stranger across the city as they are to infect their own family members.
- We assume a constant recovery rate $\gamma$. The probability of recovering in the next hour is independent of how long you have already been sick.
